title: Weddings
hook: vows before God and witnesses: for better, for worse

segments.voice: Yesterday, the blessing, and the word benediction: hands raised over a room, and people sent out the door. Your line was go in peace.

"Dearly beloved, we are gathered together here in the sight of God, and in the face of this congregation." That's how the old English prayer book opens a wedding. In front, two people who barely slept. Beside them, a best man patting his pocket for the third time to check the rings. In the second row, a grandmother crying since the processional. In a few minutes, two people will say, in front of all of them, that they'll stay through the good years and the terrible ones. Today: weddings.

Day two hundred heard Jesus on marriage; today, the wedding itself. A Christian wedding is a promise made in two directions at once: to each other, and before God. Start with the witnesses: "in the sight of God, and in the face of this congregation." The people in the pews aren't an audience. They're there to see the promise, and remember it. Then the vows. In the prayer book, each promises "to have and to hold from this day forward, for better for worse, for richer for poorer, in sickness and in health, to love and to cherish, till death us do part." Those words come from the prayer book, not the Bible. And they name the worse before it arrives. Nobody knows what's coming; the vow says yes anyway. Genesis says a man will "leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh," and in Matthew, Jesus quotes it. In John, Jesus is at a wedding in Cana when the wine runs out, and John calls what he does there the beginning of his miracles. Some couples choose Ruth's promise, "whither thou goest, I will go," which in the story Ruth says to Naomi, her mother-in-law. Churches differ. Catholics call marriage a sacrament, and in Catholic teaching the bride and groom are its ministers: they marry each other, and the priest witnesses. The Orthodox call it a holy mystery, and crowns are placed on, or held over, the couple's heads. Protestant churches that keep two sacraments, baptism and the Lord's Supper, honor marriage as holy without counting it a third.
screen: `THE VOW NAMES THE WORSE IN ADVANCE.`

segments.voice: Bring one couple to mind: newlyweds, a long-married pair, or two people in the worse part right now. Think of one thing that's hard for them and one thing that's good. If you pray, ask God to keep them in both, the better and the worse; if you don't, hold them in mind with goodwill, like a witness in the pews.
Weddings. Vows made before God and witnesses, promising in advance to stay through the better and the worse.
Your line: for better, for worse. Said out loud, with witnesses. That's day one thousand three hundred forty-six.

howItsDone: Christian couples exchange vows in church before a minister or priest and the congregation as witnesses; Catholics celebrate marriage as a sacrament, the Orthodox crown the couple in the service of crowning, and Protestant churches hold a service of worship honoring marriage as holy, without counting it a sacrament.

chat.says: Why do church weddings make such a big deal of everyone watching?
options: The guests are witnesses: they see the promise made before God, and they're there to remember it.
It's mostly for the photos; the vows matter, but the guests are just an audience.
Because the guests, not the couple, are the ones making the vows to each other.
chat.meaning: In the prayer book the wedding is "in the face of this congregation": the people aren't an audience but witnesses, there to see the promise and remember it.
